Halide organic–inorganic perovskites (HOIPs) are a promising
class of materials for neuromorphic computing and processing systems
demonstrating a variety of resistive switching (RS) mechanisms. HOIPs have
been used as active layers in two- and three-terminal synaptic devices reporting
high performance in metrics of speed and energy consumption. Nevertheless,
halide perovskites suﬀer from poor ambient stability and reproducibility. In
this work, a highly robust double memristor based on two active layers forming
a stacking heterojunction is demonstrated. In particular, the functional
layer consists of a molybdenum oxide-molybdenum sulﬁde compound
(MoO3-MoS2) and a quadruple cation perovskite (RbCsMAFA) deposited on
top showing favorable band alignment for the speciﬁc application. The double
memristor based on the MoO3-MoS2/RbCsMAFA heterojunction exhibits
impressive and stable resistive switching behavior with endurance of 100
cycles, high retention of 2 × 104 s, high environmental stability maintaining
its memristive behavior for 1 month, and excellent artiﬁcial synaptic
functions. The robust device also exhibits good thermal stability maintaining
the memristive characteristics at 85 °C, as well as good photonic memristive
behavior with an improved ON/OFF ratio under constant illumination.
Here it is proven that the proposed double memristor is a promising
candidate for artiﬁcial synapses and neuromorphic computing systems.

1. Introduction
The memory resistor commonly known
also as memristor is a two-terminal elec-
tronic component whose resistance can
be tuned by the current ﬂux ﬂowing
through it.[1–3] The device architecture
follows the metal-insulator-metal (MIM)
conﬁguration, where the “I” in the mem-
ristive device is the active layer showing
tuned resistance and the memory eﬀect
is related to the capability of these ma-
terials to modify their resistance. Mem-
ristive devices are based on the switch-
ing resistive (RS) mechanism, where
the resistance state reversibly switches
from the high resistance state (HRS)
to the low resistance state (LRS) by a
voltage application. This nonvolatile be-
havior, which is similar to biological
synapses, makes memristors appropriate
candidates for neuromorphic comput-
ing imitating the synaptic connections
in the human brain.[4,5] In the artiﬁcial
synaptic device, the top electrode serves

and the output signal is received from the “pro-synaptic neu-

oxides,[6] dichalcogenides,[7] metal nitrides,[8] metal carbides,[9]
organic materials,[10] graphene[11] and its derivatives[12] have
been used in memristive devices. In addition, halide perovskites
possess good memristive behavior, and organic–inorganic hy-
brid perovskites,[13] all-inorganic lead perovskites,[14] and lead-
free perovskites[15] have been applied to memristors.
Molybdenum disulﬁde (MoS2) is one of the most popu-
lar 2D transition metal dichalcogenides used in various appli-
cation ﬁelds such as catalysis,[16,17] optoelectronics,[18–22] and
energy,[23,24] due to its unique physical, optical, and electrical
properties.[25,26] Recently MoS2 has also been applied as an ac-
tive layer sandwiched between two electrodes in memristors,[27,28]
developed by chemical vapor deposition (CVD), mechanical ex-
foliation, etc. The MoS2-based devices showed high memristive
characteristics (retention > 104 and endurance ≈1000), whereas
synaptic plasticity has been achieved.[29,30] Furthermore, hybrid
composite materials based on MoS2 and molybdenum oxide have
been also used in memristors exhibiting promising memristive
characteristics with a high ON/OFF ratio of 200.[31] Sulfurization
of Mo2C was also proposed to obtain homogeneous Mo2C/MoS2
interfaces used as functional layers in vertical two-terminal mem-
ristor exhibiting excellent memristive behavior attributed to the
good contact between Mo2C and MoS2.[32] In another approach,
the van der Waals heterostructure consisting of diﬀerent 2D ma-
terials (i.e., MoS2 and grapheme) employed in memristor in a
stacking conﬁguration exhibited outstanding switching perfor-
mance with high endurance along with good thermal stability.[33]
Despite the extensive use of molybdenum disulﬁde in memris-
tive devices, the large-area fabrication and reproducibility repre-
sent a major disadvantage.

not only as eﬃcient active layers in optoelectronic devices but
also as functional layers in memristors exhibiting RS behavior,
due to their unique physical and structural properties such as
high charge carrier mobility, high crystallinity, bandgap tun-
ability, as well as, simple solution-processing. Among HOIPs,
CH3NH3PbI3 (MAPbI3) perovskite owns exceptional optoelec-
tronic properties making it a promising active layer in RS devices.
At any rate, MAPbI3 suﬀers from chemical and structural insta-
bility when exposed to ambient conditions. One strategy to limit
the degradation of MAPbI3 and also improve its optoelectronic
properties is the incorporation of formamidinium (CH(NH2)2
+,
FA+), cesium (Cs+), rubidium (Rb+), and mixed cations such
as MAFA+, CsMA+, RbCsMA+, and CsMAFA+ in the place of
MA+ cation.[34] On the other hand, halide perovskites suﬀer
from poor environmental stability and reproducibility. One way
to overcome these issues by postponing the degradation of the
perovskite layer due to the moisture eﬀect and thus improving
its environmental stability is the employment of interfacial layers
between the electrode and the active layer, which could be also
used as protecting layers in perovskite-based devices.[35–37]
In this work, a highly robust double memristor based on
the MoO3-MoS2/perovskite heterojunction is demonstrated. The
perovskite (RbPbI3)0.04(CsPbI3)0.05[(FAPbI3)0.85(MAPbBr3)0.15]0.91
layer with thickness of 300 nm, named hereafter as RbCsMAFA,
was deposited on MoO3-MoS2 composite thin ﬁlm of 20 nm
and the inﬂuence of two active layers forming a heterostruc-
ture on the resistive switching performance of the memristive
device was investigated. The proposed double memristor exhib-
ited good RS behavior with endurance of 100 cycles, high re-
tention of 2 × 104 s, and ON/OFF ratio of ≈102. Moreover, the
post-synaptic current (PSC) of a pair of pulses (PPF) and the
transition from short-term plasticity (STP) to long-term plasticity
(LTP) was systematically studied showing that the double mem-
ristor could be eﬀectively used as an artiﬁcial synapse emulating
the human brain. The MoO3-MoS2/RbCsMAFA-based memris-
tor also showed outstanding environmental stability with almost
unchanged memristive behavior after being stored in ambient
conditions for 1 month. Additionally, the thermal stability was
investigated. The double memristor showed good stability main-
taining the RS behavior at 85 °C. Moreover, under light stim-
ulation, an improved ON/OFF ratio was observed attributed to
the photon-to-electron conversion ability of the perovskite layer.
Overall, the double MoO3-MoS2/RbCsMAFA-based memristor
exhibited great potential for applications in neuromorphic com-
puting systems.
2. Results and Discussion

the middle of a tube furnace. A ceramic boat containing sul-
fur (S) powder was placed in the low-temperature zone of the
tube. The sulfurization temperature was set at 450 °C for 30 min
with a ﬂow of Ar/H2. After sulfurization, the resultant material

a slight shift of the spectrum toward higher binding energy values

the lattice of the metal oxide and the formation of Mo─S bonds.
Figure S1 (Supporting Information) presents the XPS spectrum
of the MoO3-MoS2 sample in the S2p region, where the doublet
with the two peaks centered at 169.1 and 170.4 eV corresponds
to oxidized sulfur (S6+)[43] produced from S2−in the sample by
sulfurization of the MoO3-x ﬁlm. The peak located at 167.1 eV is
assigned to the sulfonate[44] formed by the sulfonation reaction
between the Ar/H, S powder, and the MoO3-x ﬁlm.
Moreover, the pristine and composite material thin ﬁlms
were investigated using X-ray diﬀraction (XRD) measurement
to unravel their crystalline structure. Interestingly, a signiﬁcant
change in the crystallinity of the molybdenum oxide ﬁlm sub-
jected to sulfurization is observed, as shown in Figure 2a. Al-
though pristine MoO3-x is amorphous with no observable XRD
peaks, three sharp peaks appeared at 12.85°, 25.78° and 39.08° in
the XRD pattern of the MoO3-MoS2 composite, which are charac-
teristic of the a-ΜοΟ3 orthorhombic structure attributed to (020),
(040) and (060) crystalline planes, respectively.[45–47] More impor-
tantly, a peak at 14.43° and another one at 28.67° are also observed
corresponding to the (002) and (004) crystallographic plane of
2H-MoS2, respectively,[48] suggesting the formation of a MoO3-
MoS2 composite material upon sulfurization of the as-deposited
molybdenum oxide ﬁlm.
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis was also
employed to investigate the structure of the MoO3-MoS2 compos-
ite material. Figure 2b shows a high-resolution TEM (HRTEM)
image of a MoO3-MoS2 crystal, while the inset shows the cor-
responding fast Fourier transform (FFT) pattern. It is observed
that the FFT pattern exhibits reﬂections assigned to the 2H-
MoS2 phase, as well as, to the a-MoO3 phase in accordance
with XRD measurements. Furthermore, Figure 2c exhibits a se-
lected area from the HRTEM image (Figure 2b), where the (004)
and the (002) lattice fringes with 0.307 and 0.198 nm interpla-
nar spacings corresponding to 2H-MoS2 and a-MoO3, respec-
tively, can be seen, strongly suggesting the co-existence of both,
2H-MoS2 and a-MoO3 phase in the mixed composite material.
Figure S2 (Supporting Information) shows the high-angle annual
dark-ﬁeld (HAADF) image of the sample and the corresponding
TEM/element mapping, where the elements of Mo, S, and O are
observed suggesting that the composition of the MoO3-MoS2 is
consistent with a previously reported results.
To further testify the co-existence of MoO3 and MoS2 phases,
Raman spectroscopy was performed. In the Raman spectrum of
pristine molybdenum oxide presented in Figure 2d, no sharp
peaks appeared, conﬁrming the amorphous phase of MoO3-x
ﬁlm. The broad bands centered at 830 and 970 cm−1 are char-
acteristics of the amorphous MoO3-x attributed to the Mo2─O
and Mo═O, respectively.[49] After sulfurization, two sharp peaks
are clearly seen at 381 and 408 cm−1 attributed to E1
2 g and
A1 g modes of the MoS2, respectively, along with three weaker
peaks at 287, 818, and 994 cm−1 assigned to O═Mo═O wag-
ging mode (B2 g, B3 g), O─Mo─O symmetric stretching mode,
and Mo═O asymmetric stretching mode (Ag, B1 g), respectively
(Figure 2d).[46,50,51] Consequently, the development of mixed
MoO3-MoS2 crystals is clearly evident during the proposed sul-
furization process.
Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) measure-
ments were also performed in both samples and their FTIR spec-
tra are presented in Figure 2e. In the case of pristine MoO3-x,
a broad peak centered at 729 cm−1 and a shoulder at ≈820–
860 cm−1 is observed, attributed to the Mo─O─Mo stretching
mode, while the peak at 975 cm−1 is assigned to the Mo═O
bond.[52,53] Sulfurization of the sample caused a shift to lower fre-
quency values of the 729 cm−1 peak to 554 cm−1 and the appear-
ance of a new peak at 830 cm−1 is also observed. These two sharp
peaks refer to the terminal oxygen symmetry stretching of Mo═O
and stretching of oxygen in Mo─O─Mo bonds, respectively.[50,54]
A weaker peak at 1070 cm−1 is also observed in the FTIR spec-
trum of the MoO3-MoS2 composite sample corresponding to the
asymmetric S─O stretching mode of the sulfate species (Figure
S3, Supporting Information). Furthermore, two other peaks of
very weak intensity appeared at 622 and 484 cm−1 which can
be related to the disulﬁdes stretch (S─S), while the shoulder
centered at 527 cm−1 corresponds to the vibration mode of
MoS2.[55]
The optical properties of the composite material were also in-
vestigated using ultraviolent-visible spectroscopy. Figure S4a and
b present the transmittance and absorbance spectra, respectively,
of pristine MoO3-x and sulfurized MoO3-MoS2 ﬁlms coated on
glass substrates. An increase of transmittance (decrease of ab-
sorbance) in the visible region is observed when MoO3-x is sub-
jected to sulfurization. This change in the ﬁlm’s transmittance
is accompanied by the increase of the refractive index (RI) as
shown in Figure S4c (Supporting Information), where the RI of
the pristine MoO3-x in the visible and near-infrared region (800–
1000 nm) is ≈2, while in the case of MoO3-MoS2 composite ma-
terial the RI decreased at 450 nm (RI ≈1.9) and then increased
reaching the value of 2.5 in the near-infrared region. In addi-
tion, the MoO3-MoS2 sample exhibits an increased extinction co-
eﬃcient (Figure S4d, Supporting Information) with respect to
the pristine MoO3-x. The corresponding Tauc plots of both ﬁlms
as derived from the ellipsometry measurements are shown in
Figure 2f, where the energy bandgap values could be estimated.
In particular, the estimated indirect bandgap for the MoO3-x is
3.2 eV, while in the case of the MoO3-MoS2 composite mate-
rial, two potential bandgap values can be extracted; one of 1.4 eV
which could be attributed to the MoS2 and the other of 3.4 eV as-
cribed to MoO3. The presence of the two bandgap energies could
facilitate the charge transport/mobility in both MoS2 and MoO3
conduction bands.
The sulfurization of MoO3-x clearly aﬀected the nanomorphol-
ogy of the composite ﬁlm. Figure 2g,h shows the 5 × 5 μm2 atomic
force microscopy (AFM) images of the as-deposited and sulfur-
ized MoO3-x ﬁlms, respectively. It is observed that the surface of
the pristine MoO3-x is smooth with root mean square (RMS) sur-
face roughness of 0.41 nm, as shown in Figure 2g. In addition,
the ﬁlm is composed of small grains with dimensions of 20 nm.
On the other hand, the surface of the MoO3-MoS2 composite ma-
terial is rougher compared with the pristine MoO3-x ﬁlm with
RMS of 3.23 nm consisting also of large features with dimen-
sions > 500 nm (Figure 2h).

MoO3-MoS2 and RbCsMAFA, forming a stacked layered hetero-
junction were used as active layers. Figures S5 and S6 (Support-
ing Information) show that bare MoO3-MoS2 and RbCsMAFA
devices exhibit memory eﬀects. However, the double MoO3-
MoS2/RbCsMAFA shows distinctly pronounced memristive be-
havior. In particular, the SET-RESET voltage of FTO/MoO3-
MoS2/Al memristor is ≈±4 V, as shown in Figure S5a (Support-
ing Information), indicating that the memristive device exhibits
bipolar resistive switching behavior. The voltage +4 V refers to
a low-resistance state (LRS, i.e., ON), while the voltage −4 V is
deﬁned as high-resistance state (HRS, i.e., OFF). To verify the re-
liability of the FTO/MoO3-MoS2/Al memristor, 100 consecutive
cycles of sweep voltage from −4 to +4 V were employed on the
device (Figure S5b, Supporting Information). It is observed that
the memristor based on bare MoO3-MoS2 retained the resistive
switching behavior from SET to RESET in 100 cycles. However,
the device showed a poor ON/OFF ratio (memory window) of
≈4 (Figure S5c, Supporting Information). In the case of a bare
RbCsMAFA memristor with FTO/RbCSMAFA/Al device struc-
ture, the SET and RESET voltages are +3 and −5 V, respectively,
as shown in Figure S6a (Supporting Information). Although the
device maintains the memory eﬀect for 100 cycles, the ON/OFF
ratio is very small at ≈1.5. The symmetric current change ob-
served in both memristive devices with bare MoO3-MoS2 and
RbCsMAFA indicates that resistive switching is volatile. Inter-
estingly, the double MoO3-MoS2/RbCsMAFA/PCBM memristive
device exhibits nonvolatile resistive switching. The device shows
also excellent endurance, as presented in Figure 3c, with an im-
proved ON/OFF ratio of 125. For comparison, a memristor with-
out the PCBM buﬀer layer was also fabricated with FTO/MoO3-
MoS2/RbCsMAFA/Al device structure (Figure S7, Supporting In-
formation). Figure S7b (Supporting Information) presents the
I–V characteristic curves for 80 consecutive cycles applying
sweep voltages from −7 to +5 V, showing good endurance with
ON/OFF ratio of ≈60, which is higher than that of the bare
MoO3-MoS2 and RbCsMAFA devices. Since the memory window
of the heterojunction-based device without the PCBM is lower
compared with that of the MoO3-MoS2/RbCsMAFA/PCBM de-
vice, along with the very low ON/OFF ratio of both bare mem-
ristive devices, we can conclude that the LRS/HRS performance
of the double memristor is signiﬁcantly inﬂuenced not only
by the MoO3-MoS2/RbCsMAFA heterojunction but also by the
presence of the PCBM buﬀer layer. PCBM widely used as an
electron transport layer in organic and perovskite optoelectronic
devices[56,57] is chosen speciﬁcally to introduce a Schottky bar-
rier with the RbCsMAFA at the perovskite/Al interface. It is
suggested that the PCBM layer in conjunction with the Al
electrode is responsible for the abrupt SET process at ≈0.7 V
(Figure 3b), as opposed to the MoO3-MoS2/RbCsMAFA device
without the PCBM layer exhibiting a more gradual transition
state from ≈0.65 to 0.8 V (Figure S7, Supporting Information).
The OFF state of the MoO3-MoS2/RbCsMAFA/PCBM device
exhibits overall higher resistance than the device without the
PCBM layer resulting in stronger hysteresis and thus a higher
ON/OFF ratio. Moreover, PCBM could act as a protective layer
preventing the degradation of the perovskite ﬁlm at the RbC-
sMAFA/Al interface, creating a stable electrode Fermi level.
However, when FTO/RbCsMAFA/PCBM/Al device without the
MoO3-MoS2 layer was fabricated, a poor ON/OFF ratio of ≈1.4
was achieved (Figure S8, Supporting Information), suggesting
that the employment of the two active layers with a heterojunc-
tion structure in a double memristive device is strongly corre-
lated with the improved resistive switching performance. Conse-
quently, the double memristor with MoO3-MoS2 interfacial layer
exhibited a higher ON/OFF ratio abruptly switched from OFF to
ON state, suggesting the ﬁlament formation within the MoO3-
MoS2 ﬁlm.
Furthermore, the reproducibility of the double memristor
based on the MoO3-MoS2/RbCsMAFA heterostructure with the
PCBM buﬀer layer was investigated by estimating the cumulative
probability presented in Figure 3d. The HRS/LRS was ≈102 sug-
gesting that the memristor is reproducible during the 100 con-
secutive cycles of sweep voltage. Figure 3e shows the retention
characterization of the LRS and HRS of the double memristive
device. After the application of a SET pulse with an amplitude
of +1.3 V, a RESET pulse of −4 V, and a read voltage (Vread) of
0.1 V, the memory window of ≈2 × 103 between the LRS and
HRS of the double memristor maintained for 2 × 104s. Notably,
the endurance HRS/LRS ratio is larger than that in the retention
measurement due to the diﬀerence in the Vread.
The inﬂuence of MoO3-MoS2 thickness on the memristor per-
formance was also investigated. Therefore, memristors with the
structure FTO/MoO3-MoS2/RbCsMAFA/PCBM/Al with MoO3-
MoS2 thickness of 50 and 100 nm were fabricated. It is ob-
served that when the thickness of MoO3-MoS2 increased, the
ON/OFF ratio decreased, as shown in Figure S9 (Supporting
Information). The insertion of a thick MoO3-MoS2 layer in the
RbCsMAFA/PCBM-based memristor increased the vacancy con-
centration at the MoO3-MoS2/RbCsMAFA interface resulting in
a shorter conductive channel compared to that with the thin
(20 nm) MoO3-MoS2, and thus LRS increase and HRS decrease
occurred. The lower HRS (higher LRS) of the thicker layers-
based memristors is attributed to the excessive VS+ in the ﬁla-
ment channel during RESET (SET) operation compared to the
device with 20 nm thin MoO3-MoS2 ﬁlm. Consequently, the se-
lection of MoO3-MoS2 thickness is crucial; too high a concen-
tration of vacancies by increasing the thickness of MoO3-MoS2
may limit the performance of the RbCsMAFA/PCBM-based
memristors.
To better understand the conduction mechanism involved in
the double memristive device, log(I)-log(V) corresponding to LRS
and HRS was plotted, as shown in Figure 3f. In the case of HRS,
three diﬀerent regions are observed with slope values estimated
by performing ﬁtting curves of ≈1.1, 1.6, and 4.2, respectively.
At low voltages, the double memristive device exhibits an ohmic
behavior suggesting that the conduction resulted only from the
thermally generated free carriers. When the voltage increases,
higher current values are observed and the slope value is equal to
4.18, indicative of space-charge limited conduction mechanism
(SCLC),[58,59] which is related to charge carriers trapping and de-
trapping process. Afterward, the device is switched to LRS state
exhibiting ohmic conduction mechanism with a slope value of 1.

3. Conclusion
In summary, a highly robust double memristor based on the
MoO3-MoS2/RbCsMAFA heterojunction was fabricated. MoO3-
MoS2 composite material was developed by subjecting a thin
sub-stoichiometric molybdenum oxide to sulfurization. The op-
toelectronic and structural properties of the MoO3-MoS2 com-
posite ﬁlm were extensively investigated and its memristive be-
havior is demonstrated exhibiting good retention and endurance
and ON/OFF ratio of ≈4. On the other hand, when RbCs-
MAFA deposited on top of MoO3-MoS2 forming a stacking lay-
ered heterojunction-based memristor, an impressive ON/OFF
ratio of ≈102 was realized. The double memristive device ex-
hibited also good reproducibility (100 cycles), long data re-
tention (2 × 104 s), and excellent environmental stability

4. Experimental Section
Synthesis of MoO3-x Thin Film:
Sub-stoichiometric molybdenum ox-
ide thin ﬁlms were deposited on Si and glass substrates in a home-
made hot-wire chemical vapor deposition system (HW-CVD) consist-
ing of a stainless-steel reactor, details of which have been described
elsewhere.[67,68] MoO3-x ﬁlms were deposited using pure molybdenum
wire with a diameter of 0.5 mm (purchased from Sigma–Aldrich) and form-
ing gas (a mixture of 90% nitrogen and 10% hydrogen). Prior to the ox-
ide deposition, the substrates were cleaned with deionized water and iso-
propyl alcohol (Sigma–Aldrich), dried with a ﬂow of N2, and subjected to
UV-ozone treatment for 15 min. Subsequently, the substrates were loaded
on an aluminum susceptor, 2.5 cm below the Mo wire, which was held by
two Cu leads, and the reactor was evacuated down to 10−2 Torr using a
mechanical pump. Then, the base pressure was set at 8 × 10−2 Torr us-
ing a needle valve, and MoO3-x thin ﬁlms were deposited by heating the
Mo wire at 560 °C. Note that during the oxide deposition, the substrates
remained near room temperature.

Sigma-Aldrich) loaded in a ceramic boat was positioned at a lower temper-
ature zone (200 ± 2 °C) 14 cm away from the sample. The tube was ﬁrst
heated to 100 °C with Ar/H2 (a mixture of 95% Ar and 5% H2) ﬂow rate of
900 sccm in order to remove oxygen and moisture from the furnace. Then,

Thin Film Characterization Methods:
The surface nanomorphology of
the prepared ﬁlms was investigated by AFM measurements. AFM images
(5 × 5 μm2) were recorded using an NT-MDT AFM system in tapping
operation mode. XRD were taken using a Smart Lab Rigaku diﬀractome-
ter (𝜃/𝜃scan), manufactured in Japan in 2014 with a CuKa radiation (3
kW). Micro-Raman spectra were acquired using an inVia Raman micro-
scope equipped with an automated XYZ stage and a 532 nm solid-state
laser as the excitation source. The laser beam was focused by means of
a x50 objective on the sample surface, while the scattered beam was an-
alyzed through a 1800 lines/mm diﬀraction grating and a high-sensitivity
CCD detector. XPS measurements were carried out using a PHOIBOS 100
(SPECS) hemispherical analyzer using Mg Ka X-ray source with photon en-
ergy 1253.64 eV. Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) measure-
ments were performed with a helium excitation source with He I radia-
tion at 21.22 eV. TEM measurements were performed using a FEI Talos
F200i TEM microscope operating at 200 keV, equipped with a window-
less energy-dispersive spectroscopy microanalyzer (6 T/100 Bruker). FTIR
transmittance spectroscopy was carried out with a Bruker Tensor 27 spec-
trometer having a DTGS detector. UV–vis absorbance and transmittance
spectra were recorded through a Perkin Elmer Lambda 40 UV–vis spec-
trometer. Ellipsometry measurements were performed using a J.A Woolam
Inc. M2000F rotating compensator ellipsometer operating within the 250–
1000 nm range running the WVASE32 software at an angle of incidence of
75.14°. SEM images of the perovskite ﬁlms were recorded with a JEOL
7401f FESEM.
Device Fabrication:
MoO3-MoS2 thin ﬁlms were deposited as already
mentioned on ﬂuorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) coated on a glass substrate.
Glass/FTO substrates with sheet resistance of 10Ω/square (purchased
from Sigma–Aldrich) were cleaned following a three-step bath-cleaning
procedure; i) deionized water, ii) acetone, and iii) isopropanol bath with ul-
trasonication for 10 minutes each. After the deposition of MoO3-MoS2 the
perovskite (RbPbI3)0.04(CsPbI3)0.05[(FAPbI3)0.85(MAPbBr3)0.15]0.91 layer
named hereafter as RbCsMAFA was deposited. In particular, the
perovskite solution was prepared by mixing MABr : FAI : PbBr2 : PbI2
(0.2 : 1.14 : 0.2 : 1.24 m) in 4 : 1 v/v anhydrous DMF : DMSO. To this so-
lution, 5 vol% of 1.5 m CsI solution and 4 vol% of 1.5 m RbI solution
(both prepared in 4 : 1 vol/vol DMF : DMSO) were added. The perovskite
layer was deposited by dynamically spinning the solution on the MoO3-
MoS2 ﬁlm at 6000 rpm for 45 s. Antisolvent (200 μL, anhydrous CB, 99.8%,
Sigma–Aldrich) was dropped on the samples after 25 s of the start of the
spinning process. The as-processed perovskite ﬁlm was immediately an-
nealed at 100 °C for 45 min. The PCBM (99%, Solenne) buﬀer layer was
formed by spinning a PCBM solution with a concentration of 20 mg mL−1
in anhydrous CB at 2000 rpm for 60 s and left to dry at room temperature
for 30 min.
Electrical Characterization:
VersaSTAT 4 potentiostat was used to carry
out electrical characterizations. The Al electrode (top) was connected to
an external supply, whereas the FTO electrode (bottom) was grounded. All
the measurements were conducted at room temperature.
